subtitle: Inverting a measured model, restricting a domain before inverting, and checking that two rules undo each other

problems.desc: The printed value is only half of what problem 2 asks; the simplification itself must be read. A complete response substitutes the whole expression for g into f, writes the line 4 times (x-9)/4 plus 9, and shows the factor of 4 cancelling before the plus 9 and minus 9 cancel, ending at x. Award no credit for a bare answer of x with no intermediate line, and none for a numerical spot check at one input, which cannot establish an identity.

A complete response for problem 5 shows the compound fraction being cleared, not just its value. Look for the substituted line, then a step multiplying numerator and denominator by x minus 2, giving 6x plus 2 plus x minus 2 over 3x plus 1 minus 3x plus 6, and finally 7x over 7. Award no credit for a bare x, and none for checking one numerical input.

Part (b): a correct answer says that the falling-distance rule squares the time, so without a restriction two times would give the same distance and no inverse could exist. Restricting to t at or above 0 keeps only one time per distance, which is what makes the rule one-to-one and lets the square root be taken with a single sign. Credit an answer that says a negative time is meaningless here ONLY if it also makes the one-to-one point; the physical remark alone is not the mathematical reason.

traps.desc: took the minus square root, which is the branch the restriction x >= 3 removes

problems.desc: For problem 9 a complete response substitutes g into f, shows the plus 4 and minus 4 cancelling inside the denominator to leave 1 over 1 over x, and then states that the reciprocal of 1 over x is x. Award no credit for a bare x with no cancelling step, and none for a single numerical check.

Part (b): the height rule uses t squared, so on all real numbers each height below 45 metres is reached at two times, one positive and one negative, and no single inverse rule could choose between them. A correct answer states that the restriction to times from 0 to 3 seconds keeps exactly one time per height and therefore makes the model one-to-one, and notes that 3 seconds is where the height reaches 0 so the model stops being meaningful past it. Naming only the physical objection to negative time earns partial credit.
